create function get_next_val(seq_name varchar(128))

Serialization "isolation level" in MongoDB, or the lost-update problem


I realize MongoDB is a NoSQL solution, but I was wondering if it had some sort of equivalent to serialization-level transaction isolation level. If not, how would you solve the lost-update problem in MongoDB? I want to keep the revision history of some data in Mongo and each revision has to point to the one before it. How can I make sure no more than one latest revision exists for my data, and on the other hand that no revision is lost due to concurrent updates?

** Edit **

Oops, RTFM, it is indeed possible: http://www.mongodb.org/display/DOCS/Atomic+Operations

Not sure if I should close the question since the knowledge might be relevant to other people..

samples.general_completion:
In MongoDB, the lost-update problem can be addressed using atomic operations. These operations ensure that a sequence of read and write operations are performed as a single unit of work, guaranteeing data consistency. 

For instance, the `$inc` operator increments a value by a specified amount atomically. This means that if multiple clients attempt to increment the same value simultaneously, the operation will be executed on the latest version of the data, preventing any lost updates. 

Similarly, the `$set` operator sets a field to a specified value atomically, ensuring that concurrent updates do not overwrite each other's changes. 

Moreover, MongoDB provides the `$atomic` operator, which allows for more complex atomic operations across multiple documents or fields. This is particularly useful for maintaining revision history, where each revision points to the previous one. By using `$atomic`, you can ensure that the sequence of revisions is preserved and no updates are lost due to concurrency.

In summary, MongoDB's support for atomic operations provides a robust mechanism to handle the lost-update problem and maintain data consistency, even in a NoSQL environment. This feature, combined with proper application-level logic, enables developers to build reliable and scalable applications that can handle concurrent updates efficiently.

Why does Scala choose to have the types after the variable names? In Scala variables are declared like:

var stockPrice: Double = 100. Where the type (Double) follows the identifier (stockPrice). Traditionally in imperative languages such as C, Java, C#, the type name precedes the identifier.

double stock_price = 100.0;

Is it purely a matter of taste, or does having the type name in the end help the compiler in any way? Go also has the same style. As well as supporting type inference, this has an ergonomic benefit too. For any given variable name + type, chances are that the name is the more important piece of information.
samples.second_piece:
Moving it to the left makes it more prominent, and the code more readable once you're accustomed to the style. Other ergonomic benefits:

  • With val, var or def before member names, instead of their type, they all neatly line up in a column.
  • If you change just the type of a member, or drop it entirely in favour of inference, then a fine-grained diff tool will clearly show that the name is unaltered
  • Likewise, changing between a val/var/def is very clear in diffs
  • inference should be considered default behaviour in Scala, you only need type specifications in certain specific scenarios, even then it's mostly done for the compiler. So putting them at the very start of a declaration emphasises the wrong thing.
  • "name: Type" instead of "Type name" more closely matches the way most programmers will actually think about a declaration, it's more natural.
  • The differing C/C++ and Java conventions for pointers and arrays (i.e * being a prefix on the following name and not a suffix on the preceeding type in C/C++, or [] being a valid suffix on both names and types in Java) are still confusing to newcomers or language converts, and cause some very real errors when declaring multiple variables on a single line.   • Close the project and reopen it.

  • Check you're using the Maven installation you expect. By default m2eclipse uses the embedder, if you have a separate installation you may want to configure m2eclipse to use the external installation so that CLI and Eclipse builds are consistent. This also ensures you're configured to connect through any proxy as above.

Apple on variables: Declared Properties and Instance Variables

Make sure the name of the instance variable concisely describes the attribute stored. Usually, you should not access instance variables directly, instead you should use accessor methods (you do access instance variables directly in init and dealloc methods). To help to signal this, prefix instance variable names with an underscore (_), for example: @implementation MyClass { BOOL _showsTitle; }

ISO/IEC 9899 7.1.3 Reserved identifiers (aka C99):

  • All identifiers that begin with an underscore and either an uppercase letter or another underscore are always reserved for any use.
  • All identifiers that begin with an underscore are always reserved for use as identifiers with file scope in both the ordinary and tag name spaces. On top of that, double leading underscore is traditionally reserved for the vendor of the preprocessor / compiler / library. This avoids the case where you use __block somewhere in your code, and Apple introduces that as a new non-standard keyword. Google Objective-C Style guide:

Variable Names Variables names start with a lowercase and use mixed case to delimit words. Class member variables have trailing underscores. For example: myLocalVariable, myInstanceVariable_. Members used for KVO/KVC bindings may begin with a leading underscore iff use of Objective-C 2.0's @property isn't allowed. Google's trailing underscore doesn't force you to type one more character before Xcode fires the autocomplete, but you'll realize it is an instance variable slower if the underscore is a suffix. Leading underscore is also discouraged in C++ (see What are the rules about using an underscore in a C++ identifier?) and Core Data properties (try adding a leading underscore in the model and you'll get "Name must begin with a letter"). Whatever you chose, collisions are unlikely to happen, and if they do, you'll get a warning from the compiler. When in doubt, use the default LLVM way: @synthesize var=_var;


I own an edit of this post to reading A Motivation for ivar decorations by Mark Dalrymple. You may want to check it out.
samples.guided_completion: However, Apple does not discourage the use of the underscore prefix for instance variables. In fact, the use of the underscore prefix is a widely accepted naming convention in Objective-C for instance variables. It helps to differentiate instance variables from method names and property accessors. So, if you want to follow the common Objective-C naming conventions, you should use the underscore prefix for instance variables.

How to write good software without getting stuck

so .text and .rodata are read only so they can be in flash or ram and be used there. .data and .bss are read/write so they need to be USED in ram, but in order to put that information in ram it has to be in a non-volatile place when the power is off, then copied over to ram.

samples.general_completion:
The .text and .rodata sections are typically stored in the FLASH memory of the ATMEGA32 microcontroller. When the program starts, the microcontroller copies these sections from FLASH to RAM for execution. The .data and .bss sections are stored in both FLASH and RAM. Initially, the data is copied from the FLASH to RAM at startup. The .bss section is initialized to zero and also copied from FLASH to RAM at startup. This dual storage allows the microcontroller to maintain the data integrity even if the power is cycled, while still allowing for fast access in RAM during runtime.

In summary, the ATMEGA32 uses FLASH memory for the storage of .text, .rodata, .data, and .bss sections. At startup, the .text and .rodata are copied to RAM for execution, while the .data and .bss are copied to RAM from their initial storage in FLASH, ensuring data persistence across power cycles.

To ensure that writers aren't blocked forever by readers, readers attempting to obtain a lock will not succeed if there is a blocked writer waiting for access, even if the lock is currently only accessed by other readers. Also, if the lock is accessed by a writer and another writer comes in, that writer will have priority over any readers that might also be waiting. A secondary motivation is to explain the lack of reader-writer priority policies in shared_mutex. This is due to an algorithm credited to Alexander Terekhov which lets the OS decide which thread is the next to get the lock without caring whether a unique lock or shared lock is being sought. This results in a complete lack of reader or writer starvation. It is simply fair.

Comparing to QReadWriteLock implementation (that is write-preferring):

To ensure that writers aren't blocked forever by readers, readers attempting to obtain a lock will not succeed if there is a blocked writer waiting for access, even if the lock is currently only accessed by other readers. That's true for proposal's shared_mutex as well, to make sure writer will not wait forever if new readers are continuing to come. Also, if the lock is accessed by a writer and another writer comes in, that writer will have priority over any readers that might also be waiting. That's NOT true for proposal's shared_mutex, readers and writers have equal priorities in this case. But unfortunately final C++ Standard document doesn't contain this reference implementation. Note that despite the fact GCC contains std::shared_mutex implementation that is based on N2406 reference implementation, but on Linux it's not used by default, it uses pthread_rwlock_t from POSIX threads lib (controlled by _GLIBCXX_USE_PTHREAD_RWLOCK_T option in c++config.h). pthread_rwlock_t can be read-preferring or write-preferring depending on system setup and applied pthread attributes. See related question for details: How to prevent writer starvation in a read write lock in pthreads
samples.guided_completion: The algorithm is based on the idea of "fairness" and "priority inheritance". The basic idea is that each thread that waits for the lock gets a "ticket" (or "priority") when it starts waiting. When the lock becomes available, the thread with the highest ticket gets the lock. This ensures that no thread will wait forever, because every thread will eventually get a turn. The algorithm also ensures that threads that have been waiting longer have a higher priority, so it prevents "writer starvation" (a situation where writers are always waiting behind readers). This is a more sophisticated approach than simple "reader-writer priority" because it takes into account both the type of the lock (shared vs. unique) and the length of time each thread has been waiting. The implementation of this algorithm in the C++ standard library is based on the original proposal by Alexander Terekhov, which provides a detailed explanation of how it works and why it is a good choice for managing shared resources in a multi-threaded environment.
samples.general_completion: The std::shared_mutex implementation in the C++ Standard Library follows the algorithm proposed by Alexander Terekhov. This algorithm ensures fairness among threads competing for the lock, regardless of whether they are readers or writers. The key idea behind this approach is to let the operating system's scheduler decide which thread should acquire the lock next, without any bias towards readers or writers. This impartiality prevents both reader and writer starvation, ensuring that all threads have a fair chance to proceed with their operations. The absence of a reader-writer priority policy in std::shared_mutex is intentional and based on this fairness principle. It allows for efficient and equitable resource management, aligning with the goal of providing a robust and predictable concurrency mechanism in the C++ Standard Library.

samples.first_piece: Where does Windows PowerShell set $profile? I would like to move my default "My Documents\WindowsPowerShell" folder. However, when I try this, PowerShell of course can't find $profile.
samples.second_piece:
Is there a file or something that I can edit to point PowerShell to a different startup folder? What I can suggest is that you dot source the file having the content of your profile in the file $profile.AllUsersAllHosts

$profile.AllUsersAllHosts is something like C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\profile.ps1

Related question: Is it possible to change the default value of $profile to a new value?
samples.general_completion: The $PROFILE environment variable is used by PowerShell to locate and load the user's PowerShell profile. By default, this profile is located at "C:\Users\username\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\profile.ps1". If you want to change the location of this profile, you can do so by modifying the $PROFILE variable directly. However, it's important to note that this change will only affect the current PowerShell session. To make the change permanent, you should update the $PROFILE value in the PowerShell configuration file. This file is typically located at "C:\Users\username\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1". It involves testing the system with invalid, unexpected, or out-of-range data to determine whether the system can gracefully handle such data. Positive testing, on the other hand, involves testing the system with valid and expected data to verify that it behaves as expected under normal conditions. This type of testing helps ensure that the system meets the specified requirements and functions correctly.

In summary, positive testing focuses on confirming that the system works as intended with valid inputs, while negative testing aims to uncover errors by testing the system with invalid or unexpected inputs. First, ifelse does NOT always evaluate both expressions - only if there are both TRUE and FALSE elements in the test vector.

ifelse(TRUE, 'foo', stop('bar')) # "foo"

And in my opinion:

ifelse should not be used in a non-vectorized situation. It is always slower and more error prone to use ifelse over if / else:

# This is fairly common if/else code
if (length(letters) > 0) letters else LETTERS

# But this "equivalent" code will yield a very different result - TRY IT!
ifelse(length(letters) > 0, letters, LETTERS)

In vectorized situations though, ifelse can be a good choice - but beware that the length and attributes of the result might not be what you expect (as above, and I consider ifelse broken in that respect).

In R, is it ever faster to use a loop instead of vectorized operations? 

In general, no. Vectorized operations in R are almost always faster than loops. This is because R is designed to work with vectors, and its internal C code is optimized for vector operations.

However, there are some exceptions:

1. **Small Data**: For very small datasets, the overhead of vectorized operations might be larger than the time saved by parallel processing. In such cases, a loop might be faster.

2. **Complex Conditions**: If your loop involves complex conditions that cannot be easily vectorized, a loop might be more efficient. However, this is often a sign that your approach needs reconsideration, as R is not optimized for complex looping.

3. **Memory Efficiency**: Vectorized operations can consume more memory, especially for large datasets. In scenarios where memory is a critical constraint, a loop might be a better choice, even if it's slower.

4. **Interactivity**: For interactive use or prototyping, loops can be more intuitive and easier to debug. Once the logic is confirmed, you can then vectorize the code for performance.

5. **Specialized Packages**: Some packages provide functions optimized for specific tasks that might outperform standard vectorized operations.

samples.general_completion:
In Clojure, the `or` function does not short-circuit. This means that all arguments are evaluated, regardless of the outcome of previous ones. If you need short-circuiting behavior, you should use the `and` function instead. The `and` function in Clojure is designed to short-circuit, which means it will stop evaluating as soon as it finds a false value. 

For example, consider the following Clojure code:

(if (and (simple-function args) (not (complex-function args))) 
  (do-stuff))

If `simple-function` returns true and `complex-function` returns false, the `not` expression will return true, and `do-stuff` will be executed. The `and` function ensures that `complex-function` is not called if `simple-function` returns true, thus saving computation.

So, if you want to ensure that expensive or side-effect-heavy functions are not called unnecessarily, you should use `and` instead of `or` in Clojure. This behavior aligns with the principle of "lazy evaluation" that Clojure embraces, optimizing for performance and minimizing unnecessary computations.

Therefore, if you need to access specific parts of a compressed file randomly, you should consider using a different compression method that supports random access, such as a format that includes a table of contents or index. Alternatively, you could store the compressed data in a structured format that allows for random access, such as a database or a file system that supports seeking to specific positions.

When switching files using the minibuffer (C-x C-f), I often use M-Backspace to delete words in the path. Emacs automatically places what I delete into the kill ring. This can be annoying, as sometime I am moving to another file to paste something, and I end up pasting part of the file path. samples.second_piece:
Emacs doesn't have a backward-delete-word function, but it's easy enough to define one:

(defun backward-delete-word (arg)
  "Delete characters backward until encountering the beginning of a word. With argument ARG, do this that many times."
  (interactive "p")
  (delete-region (point) (progn (backward-word arg) (point))))

Then you can bind M-Backspace to backward-delete-word in minibuffer-local-map:

(define-key minibuffer-local-map [M-backspace] 'backward-delete-word)

Here's how you can do it:

1. Press `M-x` to open the `M-x` command prompt.
2. Type `customize-variable` and press `Enter`.
3. In the `Variable` field, type `minibuffer-auto-kill-function` and press `Enter`.

Another developer then pulls from the server from the same branch (allegedly seeing my changes, as far as I'm aware), makes some modifications, commits them to their own local copy then finally pushes it back to the server. Somewhere in the middle of doing this my changes get lost as their push (326c8fd0...) causes a merge with lots of delete/add lines resetting the repository back to a much older revision. This has happened a few times now even with fresh copies of the repository. The highlighted line below (8def6e9..) was a commit I made, the following commits should have been on this same branch assuming the other developer pulled the changes. A merge happens at 326c8fd0 which ends up resetting the repository incorrectly, losing previous changes. TortoiseGit log

Am I missing something very obvious as to why this is happening? We're both using TortoiseGit. Sorry for the probably vague explanation. In your example, someone is merging f36908d (the first parent; their HEAD at the time of the merge) and 8def6e9 (the second parent; probably the tip of the origin branch at the time of the merge) to produce 326c8fd0. If the merge commit (326c8fd0) is missing significant pieces of content with respect to either of its parents (f36908d and 8def6e9; you say it is missing pieces of the latter), then whoever create the merge commit is probably executing the merge in an inappropriate fashion.
samples.second_piece:
This person may be using the ours merge strategy (merge or pull with -s ours/--strategy=ours), the ours option to the default recursive merge strategy (merge or pull with -X ours/--strategy-option=ours), or they may just be making bad decisions when manually resolving the merge conflicts. The ours strategy completely ignores any content changes made in the history all parents but the first. You can usually identify this type of merge because the merge commit and its first parent (i.e. their changes) will have identical trees (i.e. git diff f36908d 326c8fd0 would show no differences). The ours merge strategy option will also ignore changes from the history of the second parent (i.e. your changes), but only those that conflict with changes made in the history of the first parent (i.e. their changes). In this case, some changes from the second parent may make it into the result, but others may be dropped entirely. The other likely alternative is that they are just making bad decisions while resolving conflicts generated during a default merge. Either way, someone will probably have to talk to the user that did the merge to find out exactly what they did, and why they did it so that a policy can be devised to prevent the problem in the future. To recover, you might redo the merge yourself and them merge the result into the current tip of the history:

git checkout -b remerge f36908d
git merge 8def6e9
# resolve conflicts and commit
git checkout develop
git merge remerge
# maybe resolve more conflicts

# eventually: git branch -d remerge

Or, if you are okay with rewriting history:

git checkout -b remerge f36908d
git merge 8def6e9
# resolve conflicts and commit
git rebase --onto remerge 326c8fd0 develop
# maybe more conflicts to resolve at each rebased commit

samples.general_completion:
However, they are not universal in the sense that they can't handle every possible language requirement. For example, regular expressions can't handle recursive patterns or count the number of nested parentheses. This is because regular expressions are based on finite automata, which are not capable of counting or handling recursion. 

In contrast, formal language theory distinguishes between regular languages and context-free languages. Regular expressions are well-suited for matching patterns in regular languages, but they fall short when it comes to context-free languages, which require more powerful tools like parsers.

Therefore, while regular expressions are a versatile and widely-used tool across many programming languages, they are not a universal solution for all language processing needs. Depending on the complexity of the language requirements, other approaches may be necessary.

In addition to automatically incrementing the version number upon check-in, it is also possible to configure Team Foundation Server (TFS) to execute a script that updates the version number in the project files. This feature can be particularly useful for ensuring consistency across multiple files or for implementing more complex versioning schemes. 

To achieve this, you can leverage TFS's built-in extensibility features, specifically the "Check-in Policies" and "Custom Build Activities". 

**Check-in Policies** allow you to define rules that must be met before a check-in is accepted. You can create a policy that triggers a script to update the version numbers in your project files whenever a check-in is attempted. This script can be written in PowerShell, C#, or any other language supported by TFS.

**Custom Build Activities** provide another avenue for automating tasks. While primarily designed for build processes, they can also be adapted to run during check-in operations. A custom build activity can be configured to execute your version increment script, ensuring that the version numbers are updated consistently across all relevant files.

By combining these features, you can create a robust system that not only increments the version number automatically with each check-in but also ensures that your versioning scheme is consistently applied across your project files.

I would really like to reuse my existing ViewModels but since both Android and iOS seem to have no such thing as XAML's strong databinding I would like to ask if anyone went that route before and can recommend some best practices or existing solutions. We're doing this with an application right now, but writing for iOS first (even before Windows). It is not full of rainbows and ponies for sure. I would recommend the following:

  • Use a MVVM framework on Windows that doesn't require you to expose ICommand on every action the user takes (like Caliburn, for example), it also shouldn't require a dependency to it from within all of your ViewModels.
  • Conditionally inherit the WPF-specific pieces of your ViewModelBase class, you can do this with partial classes or an #if iPhone directive. INotifyPropertyChanged or ICommand are examples.
  • Use an IoC container, it is very helpful to abstract out things like saving settings to the filesystem which will be very different on all platforms. Also helps to sort out your dependencies as well, which is very helpful for separating out platform-specific code from non-platform specific.
  • Use a "messenger" of some kind (example here), usually included with an MVVM framework. This is a must in my opinion, at least for iOS. Apple's MVC is so all over the place, it's better to have global messages you can subscribe to in a weak referenced (and decoupled) way.
  • Use MVC on each platform like you would natively, then treat each ViewModel as you would if you were calling it manually. There are no UI bindings, no ICommand, so keep your ViewModel's simple.
  • Linking files is the best trick ever.

The Subversion command `svn revert` is used to undo changes to your working copy. By default, it only reverts changes to the files in the current directory and below. To revert all files in your working copy, you can use the `-R` flag, which stands for "recursive". This flag tells `svn revert` to apply the revert operation to all files in the current directory and all of its subdirectories.

Here's how you can use it:

```
svn revert -R .
```

This command will revert all changes in your working copy back to the last committed version. It effectively undoes all modifications, additions, and deletions made since the last update from the repository.

It's important to note that `svn revert` does not communicate with the repository to retrieve the latest version of the files. Instead, it reverts your local changes to the last state of your working copy. If you want to get the latest version from the repository, you should use `svn update`:

```
svn update
```

This command fetches the latest changes from the repository and merges them into your working copy. If there are conflicts, `svn update` will inform you and allow you to resolve them manually.

List<string> myList = new List<string> { "Item1", "Item2", "Item3" };

samples.general_completion:
The **.class pattern does not work with the forget command. Instead, you should use the --include option with a regular expression that matches the files you want to forget. Here's how you can do it:

```bash
hg forget --include='.*\.class$'
```

This command tells Mercurial to forget all files that end with `.class`. The `.*` is a regular expression that matches any characters (including none), and `\.` matches a literal dot. The `$` indicates the end of the line. This pattern will match any file that has `.class` as its extension, regardless of the file name.

If you want to ensure that only files in the current directory are matched, you can use:

```bash
hg forget --include='*.class'
```

This pattern matches any file that ends with `.class` in the current directory. 

Remember to run `hg commit -m "Forget .class files"` after running the `forget` command to permanently remove these files from the repository history.

samples.second_piece: The question mark is just a shorthand. Nullable is a struct, and therefore is a value type. Since it retains a reference to the Foo struct, you still have a circular reference consisting of value types.
samples.general_completion:
So, when you declare a Foo? bar; inside a struct, you're actually declaring a Nullable<Foo> bar;.

This means that bar is a struct that contains a bool (hasValue) and a Foo (value). This struct is then placed on the stack, and it's this struct that's nullable, not the Foo inside it.

Therefore, if you were to set bar = null; (which is equivalent to bar = default(Foo?);), you're actually setting bar.hasValue to false and bar.value to default(Foo), which is a default-initialized Foo instance.

This default-initialized Foo instance is not null; it's just uninitialized. It has a default value for all its members, which is not the same as null.

So, in summary, a nullable value type is a struct that contains a value type and a boolean indicating whether the value type has a value. It's this struct that's nullable, not the value type inside it.

In MongoDB, when you perform an update operation, it returns a document that includes information about the operation. This document includes a field called "n", which represents the number of documents that were matched and updated by the operation.

For example, if you execute an update operation like this:

```javascript
db.collection.updateMany({ "condition": "value" }, { $set: { "field": "newValue" } })
```

After running this command, you can check the result to see how many documents were updated. The result will look something like this:

```json

```

In this example, "nModified" indicates that 3 documents were successfully updated. This is the information you're looking for to determine the number of updated documents.
